speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The PQs will be answered by the Ministers from the relevant Ministry and thereafter, for supplementary PQs to be asked.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And with your permission, may I take Question Nos 4 and 5 together now?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Members have asked questions about various lapses and irregularities highlighted in the AGO report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government’s approach to governance is one of responsibility, transparency and accountability.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To that end, we have put in place governance structures at the whole-of-Government (WOG) and agency levels to ensure proper accountability for the use of public funds.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the WOG level, we have rules and guidelines on financial controls for public agencies carrying out finance functions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Central agencies such as the Smart Nation and Digital Government Group (SNDGG) and Grants Governance Office in the Ministry of Finance (MOF) oversee common functional areas and work with agencies to ensure robust internal controls.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOF has recently set up the Government Procurement Function Office.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also ongoing efforts to review policies and processes and strengthen capabilities, particularly for more complex areas such as IT and construction.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the agency level, enterprise risk management and system controls are in place.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The management of development projects and facility management are specialised areas requiring deeper technical expertise and experience.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition to raising the capabilities of our officers, agencies are enhancing supervision of contractors and managing agents.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The AGO is an important part of our system of checks to uncover weaknesses and shortcomings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGO adopts a risk-based approach in determining which areas to cover in an audit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: AGO takes into consideration factors such as materiality and potential impact.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Areas selected for audit could include areas with higher value expenditure, higher volume of transactions and key IT systems that deal with financial transactions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, as part of AGO’s annual audit of the Government Financial Statements, it examines the controls in place for payments to government suppliers and also audits the key IT systems used to process financial transactions, including those administered by MOF.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given the scale and complexity of Government operations it would be unrealistic to expect zero lapses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With 150,000 officers in the Public Service handling hundreds of thousands of transactions each year and more than 2,000 Government IT systems built over the years by different vendors and using different technologies, human errors and process gaps will occur from time to time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Given this, what is important, therefore, is that we must have the means to pick up such lapses and address them in an upfront and transparent manner.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The annual AGO report and other elements of our governance system outlined earlier function as regular “health checks” for the Public Service and allows it to take corrective and preventive actions as may be necessary.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Yip asked about the types of recurring lapses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These have typically been in the areas of procurement and contracts management, IT controls and grants management, which share common factors like the scale and complexity of operations, a constantly changing operating environment, high volume of transactions and multiple touchpoints.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These are the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Education (MOE), MOF, the Ministry of Health and the People’s Association (PA).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The lapses arose from gaps in agency processes and human factors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To mitigate the risks associated with IT and our digitalisation efforts, we are deploying more central IT infrastructure and common services, which facilitate regular reviews at the WOG level.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: SNDGG is implementing central tools to automate agencies’ review of privileged users’ activities and management of user accounts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Agencies regularly review and strengthen their own processes and systems to mitigate agency-level risks.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the Accountant-General's Department has taken steps to enhance IT security and will be adopting the central tools to automate the review of privileged users' activities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, MOF has established the Finance and Procurement Academy, in partnership with the Civil Service College, to better equip public officers with relevant competencies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Officers involved in finance, procurement and contract management receive refreshers and updates on policies and practices.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will step up our efforts as the recent audit findings pertain to more complex types of procurement and contract management, particularly in the areas of IT and development projects.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Officers involved in IT roles are actively engaged on audit findings as well as learning points and ways to prevent lapses.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Agencies have also stepped up the training of these officers to strengthen IT governance and security processes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Singh asked what actions are being taken in respect of the irregularities in the records furnished for audit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Government takes a serious view of such irregularities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Public officers found guilty of misconduct face disciplinary actions, depending on the nature, extent and circumstances of the breaches.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Public officers from two agencies, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) and PA, were investigated for the fabrication of records.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, while the claims were real, the conduct of the officers in fabricating the claims records was wrong.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The officers involved have been suspended from duties pending the outcome of the investigations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs had three cases of possible irregularities in records furnished by contractors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In two cases, Police reports were lodged and the investigations have been completed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: One contractor was charged in Court and the other was given a 12-month conditional warning.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the third case, action has been taken against the contractor for non-compliance of contractual requirements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There was no fabrication of records by public officers in any of these three cases.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, two officers are undergoing internal investigations for the lack of due diligence.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the remaining two agencies, MOE and the Housing and Development Board, investigations are ongoing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Appropriate action will be taken depending on the outcome of the investigations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Integrity is a core value of the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We will continue to uphold strict standards in ensuring accountability in the use of public funds.
